pe.path: Applied Sciences > Food Science > Development of Sensory Lexicons
pe.note: Labels and one-line meanings taken read-only from Project Everything's built-in Food Science subtree (TOPIC_SUBDIVISIONS + node summaries in src/App.jsx). Ordering mild to intense was added here.

sensory.name: Standard sensory-science vocabulary
sensory.note: Gap-fill entries written for this site from common sensory-evaluation, flavor-wheel and taste-physiology vocabulary where Project Everything has no node.

categories.label: Taste
categories.summary: The basic chemical sensations detected by taste receptors on the tongue.

children.label: Sweet
children.summary: A taste quality associated with sugars and perceived as pleasant and desirable.
children.science: Sugars such as sucrose and fructose (and sweeteners) bind the T1R2/T1R3 sweet receptor.

children.label: Sweetness
children.summary: How sweet it is, from a faint hint to too much.

scale.meaning: Only a hint of sweetness, just enough to soften acidity or bitterness.
examples: cold-brew coffee with a dash of milk

scale.meaning: A soft, understated sweetness that is gentle and unassuming.
A straightforward, clean sweetness like table sugar.
scale.science: Sucrose: the reference sweetness most sweeteners are rated against.

scale.meaning: An intense, confectionery sweetness like hard candy.
So sweet it becomes heavy, tiring or unpleasant.
examples: pecan pie with syrup on top

children.label: Kinds of Sweet
children.summary: What the sweetness tastes like, from light and clean to dark, heavy or artificial.

scale.meaning: A light, juicy sweetness like ripe fruit, quick to fade.
scale.science: Fructose tastes sweeter than sucrose but peaks and fades faster.

scale.meaning: A warm, floral sweetness characteristic of honey.
A rounded, woody, vanilla-tinged sweetness like maple syrup.
A dark, deep sweetness with a bittersweet, mineral edge, like treacle or blackstrap.
An artificial-sweetener sweetness that lingers with a slightly bitter or metallic edge.
scale.science: High-potency sweeteners often also trigger bitter receptors, giving a lingering, artificial edge.

children.label: Sour
children.summary: A taste quality caused by acids, creating a sharp, tart sensation on the palate.

children.label: Sourness
children.summary: How sour it is, from a gentle tang to mouth-puckering.

scale.meaning: A lively, stimulating sourness with a pleasant bite.
A pleasantly sharp, mouth-watering sourness.
A clean, sharp sourness from high acid content.
An intense, penetrating sourness that stands out prominently.
An intense sourness that makes the mouth pucker and water.

children.label: Kinds of Sour
children.summary: Which acid the sourness tastes like, from soft and rounded to pungent.

scale.meaning: A soft, rounded, creamy sourness like yogurt, buttermilk or sourdough.
scale.science: Lactic acid from fermentation by lactic acid bacteria.

scale.meaning: A crisp, juicy sourness like green apples or rhubarb.
scale.science: Malic acid, as in green apples and cherries.

scale.meaning: A bright, clean sourness that hits fast and fades fast, like lemon or lime juice.
scale.science: Citric acid.

scale.meaning: A hard, firm, lingering sourness like grapes, wine or tamarind.
scale.science: Tartaric acid, the main acid in grapes and tamarind.

scale.meaning: A pungent, sharp sourness you can smell as well as taste.
scale.science: Acetic acid is volatile, so it is smelled as well as tasted.

children.label: Salty
children.summary: A taste quality caused by sodium ions, enhancing other flavors and adding savory depth.

scale.meaning: Flat and in need of salt; the other flavors do not come forward.
A balanced, well-distributed saltiness that enhances overall flavor.
A clean, neutral saltiness resembling dissolved sea salt.
A strong, mineral saltiness like seawater, olives or pickle brine.
Salt dominates and masks the other flavors; harsh at the back of the tongue.
examples: instant ramen with the whole packet
salt cod not soaked long enough
scale.science: At high concentrations salt also activates sour and bitter cells, which is why too much salt tastes harsh.

children.label: Bitter
children.summary: A taste quality often from alkaloids and polyphenols; pleasant in small doses, harsh at high levels.

children.label: Bitterness
children.summary: How bitter it is, from gently bittersweet to acrid.

scale.meaning: A gentle bitterness balanced by sweetness, as in dark chocolate or marmalade.
A clean, invigorating bitterness that wakes up the palate, as in an aperitif.
A sharp bitterness with an assertive, stinging quality.
A rough, aggressive bitterness that lacks finesse.
A harsh, irritating bitterness that is unpleasant and sharp, often burnt.
examples: scorched coffee left on the hotplate

children.label: Kinds of Bitter
children.summary: Where the bitterness seems to come from, from mild to most assertive.

scale.meaning: The mild bitterness of citrus pith and peel, like grapefruit or marmalade.
scale.science: Nootkatone (grapefruit) and bitter flavonoids such as naringin.

scale.meaning: A leafy, vegetal bitterness like endive, radicchio, kale or dandelion.
A resinous, lingering bitterness like a hoppy beer.
scale.science: Iso-alpha acids formed when hops are boiled.

scale.meaning: A bitter quality reminiscent of medicine, tonic or bitter herbs.
scale.science: Quinine in tonic water is the classic example.

children.label: Umami
children.summary: A savory taste quality caused by glutamates, adding depth and richness to food.
children.science: Glutamate, boosted by inosinate (meat, fish) and guanylate (dried mushrooms): together they multiply the savory effect.

scale.meaning: A subtle, complex umami that reveals itself gradually.
A clear, mouth-filling savoriness, like a well-made sauce.
A warm, savory umami quality like a rich stock or soup base.
Savory enough that you keep wanting another bite.
A deep, intense savoriness like reduced stock, aged parmesan or soy sauce.

children.label: Mineral
children.summary: Mineral and metallic taste sensations beyond the five basic tastes, from neutral to most assertive.

scale.meaning: A neutral, flat taste quality with no distinct flavor profile.
A faint stony impression, like spring water or some white wines.
A chalky, mineral taste associated with calcium-rich foods and hard water.
A taste reminiscent of metal, like a coin or blood.
examples: food left in an opened tin
scale.science: Iron and copper ions, and oxidized fats, are common causes.

categories.label: Aroma
categories.summary: The volatile chemical compounds released by food perceived through the nose, contributing significantly to flavor.

children.label: Fruity
children.summary: Aromas reminiscent of fresh or cooked fruits, typically sweet and pleasant.
children.science: Mostly esters, aldehydes and terpenes released as fruit ripens.

children.label: Citrus
children.summary: Bright, sharp aromas from citrus fruits dominated by limonene and citral compounds.

scale.meaning: A warm, sweet citrus aroma reminiscent of fresh orange peel.
scale.science: Limonene dominates orange peel oil.

scale.meaning: A bright, zesty aroma characteristic of fresh lemon peel and juice.
scale.science: Citral gives lemon its sharper note.

scale.meaning: A green, sharper citrus aroma, slightly floral.
A tangy, slightly sulfury citrus aroma with a bitter-peel edge.
scale.science: Nootkatone and a trace of sulfur thiols.

scale.meaning: A sharp, peel-oil burst of citrus that is lively and refreshing.
examples: lime zest grated over a dish
a twisted lemon peel over a drink

children.label: Berry
children.summary: Aromas resembling fresh berries, typically sweet and slightly tart.

scale.meaning: A mild, sweet-tart aroma reminiscent of fresh blueberries.
A sweet, fruity aroma characteristic of fresh strawberries.
scale.science: Furaneol gives strawberries their sweet, caramel-like note.

scale.meaning: A perfumed, tangy berry aroma.
scale.science: Raspberry ketone.

scale.meaning: A dark, juicy, slightly earthy berry aroma.
An intense, dark, slightly leafy berry aroma, like cassis.

children.label: Tropical
children.summary: Rich, sweet aromas evocative of tropical fruits.

scale.meaning: A sweet, slightly starchy aroma characteristic of ripe bananas.
scale.science: Isoamyl acetate.

scale.meaning: A delicate, rose-scented tropical aroma.
scale.science: Rose oxide, the same compound that scents roses.

scale.meaning: A sweet, lush aroma reminiscent of ripe mango.
A bright, sweet-tart aroma characteristic of fresh pineapple.
An intensely tropical, almost sulfury-sweet aroma.
scale.science: Sulfur-containing thiols contribute the 'catty' tropical punch.

children.label: Apple & Pear
children.summary: Fresh aromas of apples, pears and quince.

scale.meaning: A soft, sweet, slightly floral fruit aroma.
A fresh, clean fruity aroma reminiscent of ripe red apples.
A sharp, tart, crunchy apple aroma.
scale.science: Acetaldehyde and hexyl acetate; a known off-flavor in young beer.

scale.meaning: A heady, perfumed, honeyed fruit aroma.

children.label: Stone Fruit
children.summary: Lush aromas of fruit with a pit: peaches, apricots, plums and cherries.

scale.meaning: A lush, ripe, soft stone-fruit aroma.
scale.science: Lactones such as gamma-decalactone.

scale.meaning: A tangier, more concentrated stone-fruit aroma.
A dark, deep, juicy stone-fruit aroma.
A sharp, sweet stone-fruit aroma with an almond-like edge.
scale.science: Benzaldehyde, shared with almonds.

children.label: Cooked & Dried
children.summary: Fruit aromas concentrated by cooking or drying, from lightly stewed to deep and dark.

scale.meaning: Soft, gently cooked fruit, like a compote.
A concentrated, cooked-berry aroma like jam or very ripe fruit.
A sweet, concentrated dried-grape aroma.
A deep, honeyed, seedy dried-fruit aroma.
A dark, intense, slightly bitter dried-plum aroma.

children.label: Floral
children.summary: Aromas reminiscent of flowers, typically light, fragrant, and delicate.

children.label: Light Florals
children.summary: Fresh, airy flower aromas, from a faint hint to sweet nectar.

scale.meaning: A faint, fresh hint of flowers.
A light, fresh, slightly grapey floral aroma.
A soft, honeyed, apple-like floral aroma.
A sweet, bright floral aroma, like neroli or orange-flower water.
scale.science: Linalool and methyl anthranilate.

scale.meaning: A sweet, nectar-rich floral aroma.

children.label: Heady Florals
children.summary: Rich, strong flower aromas, from powdery to perfume-like.

scale.meaning: A soft, powdery, sweet floral aroma.
scale.science: Ionones, also found in raspberries.

scale.meaning: A sweet, fragrant aroma characteristic of rose petals.
scale.science: Geraniol and 2-phenylethanol.

scale.meaning: A cool, herbal-floral aroma characteristic of lavender flowers.
A sweet, intensely floral aroma characteristic of jasmine flowers.
An intense floral aroma that is strong and reminiscent of perfume; soapy when overdone.

children.label: Spice
children.summary: Aromas from spices and aromatic compounds that are warm, pungent, or stimulating.

children.label: Sweet Spices
children.summary: Warm baking-spice aromas, from soft vanilla to intense clove.

scale.meaning: A soft, sweet, creamy aroma like vanilla pods or custard.
scale.science: Vanillin, also released from oak barrels.

scale.meaning: A warm, soft, slightly woody spice aroma.
A bright, cool, eucalyptus-tinged spice aroma.
scale.science: 1,8-cineole, the eucalyptus compound.

scale.meaning: A warm, sweet spicy aroma characteristic of cinnamon bark.
scale.science: Cinnamaldehyde.

scale.meaning: An intense, warm, eugenol-rich aroma characteristic of dried cloves.
scale.science: Eugenol.

children.label: Savory Spices
children.summary: Earthy, seedy spice aromas used in savory cooking, from light to heavy.

scale.meaning: A light, citrusy, slightly floral seed-spice aroma.
A sweet licorice aroma like fennel seed, star anise or tarragon.
scale.science: Anethole.

scale.meaning: A warm, earthy, slightly sweaty spice aroma.
scale.science: Cuminaldehyde.

scale.meaning: A heavy, savory blend of toasted spice with a maple-like fenugreek note.
scale.science: Sotolon from fenugreek, which smells of maple and curry.

children.label: Pungent Spices
children.summary: Sharp, hot-smelling spice aromas, from warm ginger to nose-tingling mustard.

scale.meaning: A warm, zesty, lemony spice aroma like fresh ginger.
A sharp, woody, nose-tickling aroma like freshly ground black pepper.
scale.science: Terpenes plus rotundone give the aroma; piperine gives the bite.

scale.meaning: The green-fruity or smoky-roasted smell of chili peppers.
scale.science: Pyrazines and esters; capsaicin itself has no smell.

scale.meaning: A sharp, sinus-prickling aroma like mustard, horseradish or wasabi.
scale.science: Allyl isothiocyanate, formed when the plant cells are crushed.

children.label: Green & Herbal
children.summary: Green, plant-like aromas from fresh vegetables and herbs, fresh or dried.

children.label: Green & Vegetal
children.summary: Fresh-cut plant and vegetable aromas, from light cucumber to pungent green pepper.

scale.meaning: A light, cool, watery green aroma like cucumber or melon rind.
scale.science: Nonadienal.

scale.meaning: A soft, sweet aroma of dried grass.
scale.science: Coumarin.

scale.meaning: A fresh, green aroma reminiscent of cut grass or fresh herbs.
scale.science: 'Green leaf volatiles' such as cis-3-hexenol, released when leaves are cut.

scale.meaning: A sharp, green, slightly bitter aroma like tomato vines.
A strong, pungent green aroma like raw bell pepper or unripe wine grapes.
scale.science: Methoxypyrazines, detectable at parts per trillion.

children.label: Fresh Herbs
children.summary: Soft, leafy herb aromas, from mild parsley to piercing mint.

scale.meaning: A mild, clean, green herb aroma.
A fresh, sweet, slightly anise herb aroma.
A sweet, slightly anise-tinged herbal aroma characteristic of fresh basil.
scale.science: Linalool and estragole.

scale.meaning: A bright, citrusy herb aroma that some people find soapy.
scale.science: Aldehydes such as decenal; a smell-receptor variant makes them read as soap.

scale.meaning: A cool, menthol-rich aroma characteristic of mint leaves.
scale.science: Menthol (peppermint) or carvone (spearmint).

children.label: Woody Herbs
children.summary: Resinous herb aromas, mostly from dried or woody-stemmed herbs, from mild to piney.

scale.meaning: A mild, sweet, slightly floral background herb aroma.
A warm, savory, slightly medicinal herb aroma.
scale.science: Thymol.

scale.meaning: A warm, earthy herbal aroma characteristic of dried oregano.
scale.science: Carvacrol and thymol.

scale.meaning: A strong, musky, slightly camphor herb aroma.
A resinous, sharp, piney herb aroma.
scale.science: Pinene and camphor.

children.label: Onion & Garlic
children.summary: Sulfur-rich aromas of the onion family, from mild chive to raw garlic.

scale.meaning: A mild, fresh, green onion aroma.
A soft, sweet, cooked-onion aroma.
A sharp, sulfurous onion aroma.
A pungent, strong garlic aroma.
scale.science: Allicin, formed when garlic is crushed.

children.label: Nutty & Grainy
children.summary: Warm, rich aromas of nuts, seeds, grains and baked bread.

children.label: Fresh Nuts
children.summary: Raw or lightly toasted nut aromas, from mild coconut to intense almond.

scale.meaning: A sweet, creamy, tropical nut aroma.
scale.science: Delta-lactones.

scale.meaning: A mild, buttery, sweet nut aroma.
A rich nut aroma with a tannic, slightly bitter skin.
A sweet, slightly bitter aroma characteristic of almonds and marzipan.
scale.science: Benzaldehyde.

children.label: Roasted Nuts & Seeds
children.summary: Toasted nut and seed aromas, from buttery pecan to deep sesame.

scale.meaning: A soft, buttery, toasted nut aroma.
A warm, toasty aroma characteristic of roasted hazelnuts.
scale.science: Filbertone.

scale.meaning: A rich, earthy aroma characteristic of roasted peanuts.
scale.science: Roasting pyrazines.

scale.meaning: A deep, intensely roasted seed aroma like sesame oil or tahini.

children.label: Grain & Bread
children.summary: Cereal and baked aromas, from raw grain to dark crust.

scale.meaning: A mild, raw-grain aroma like oats, porridge or flour.
A sweet, grainy aroma like malted milk, malt loaf or beer wort.
scale.science: Maltol and other compounds from kilned barley.

scale.meaning: The soft, yeasty aroma of a fresh loaf’s crumb.
A dry, lightly toasted baked aroma like crackers or shortbread.
The deep, roasty aroma of a dark bread crust.
scale.science: Maillard products such as 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline.

children.label: Roasted & Caramelized
children.summary: Aromas produced by the Maillard reaction, caramelization and smoke during cooking.

children.label: Caramel
children.summary: Aromas of cooked sugar, from pale butterscotch to burnt sugar.

scale.meaning: A pale, sweet, buttery cooked-sugar aroma.
A rich, warm sweetness from caramelized sugars during cooking.
scale.science: Sugars broken down by heat alone (no protein needed), giving furanones and maltol.

scale.meaning: A deep, dark, slightly bitter cooked-sugar aroma.
A dark, bitter-edged sugar aroma, like the top of a crème brûlée.

children.label: Roast
children.summary: Browning aromas from high-heat cooking, from lightly toasted to burnt.

scale.meaning: A mild, nutty aroma from light browning of grains or bread.
A complex, savory-sweet, nutty aroma from Maillard browning, like seared meat or brown butter.
scale.science: Maillard reactions between amino acids and sugars.

scale.meaning: A deep, warm aroma from high-heat oven or pan roasting.
A bitter, smoky edge from heavy browning at the surface.
An acrid char smell meaning the food has been overcooked or burned.
examples: the burnt bits at the bottom of a pan

children.label: Cocoa & Coffee
children.summary: Roasted-bean aromas, from sweet chocolate to dark espresso.

scale.meaning: A sweet, rounded milk-chocolate aroma.
A dry, dark, slightly bitter cocoa-powder aroma.
A deep, roasted coffee aroma.
scale.science: 2-furfurylthiol, the key roasted-coffee compound.

scale.meaning: A concentrated, dark-roast, bittersweet coffee aroma.

children.label: Smoke
children.summary: Aromas of wood and peat smoke, from a gentle whiff to tarry.

scale.meaning: A gentle aroma of wood smoke, as in smoked fish or cheese.
scale.science: Guaiacol and other phenols from burning lignin.

scale.meaning: A strong, resinous woodsmoke aroma, like barbecue or a log fire.
A dry, stale smoke aroma, like an ashtray or cold embers.
A medicinal, iodine-tinged smoke, as in Islay whisky.
scale.science: Cresols and other phenols from burning peat.

scale.meaning: A heavy, oily, creosote-like smoke aroma.

children.label: Earthy & Woody
children.summary: Aromas reminiscent of wood, soil, and earthy natural materials.

children.label: Soil & Forest
children.summary: Aromas of soil, fungi and the forest floor, from leafy to intense truffle.

scale.meaning: A complex earthy aroma evoking the smell of a forest floor.
An earthy, umami-adjacent aroma characteristic of mushrooms.
scale.science: 1-octen-3-ol, the 'mushroom alcohol'.

scale.meaning: A damp-soil aroma, like beets or fresh rain on dirt.
scale.science: Geosmin, which humans detect at parts per trillion.

scale.meaning: An intense, musky, slightly garlicky earthy aroma.
scale.science: Dimethyl sulfide and related sulfur compounds.

children.label: Wood
children.summary: Aromas of wood and dried leaf, from light cedar to tobacco.

scale.meaning: A light, dry, pencil-shaving wood aroma.
A warm wood aroma with vanilla and toast, from oak barrels.
scale.science: Vanillin and oak lactones from barrel aging.

scale.meaning: A sticky, sappy wood aroma like pine resin.
scale.science: Pinene and other terpenes.

scale.meaning: A dry, sweet, leafy aroma like pipe tobacco or cigar box.

children.label: Savory & Fermented
children.summary: Aromas of dairy, meat and the sea, and of yeast and fermentation, ranging from pleasant to off-putting.

children.label: Dairy
children.summary: Milk, butter and cheese aromas, from fresh milk to stinky cheese.

scale.meaning: A mild, fresh, sweet aroma of milk or cream.
A rich, creamy aroma characteristic of butter and cream.
scale.science: Diacetyl.

scale.meaning: A tangy dairy aroma like yogurt, sour cream or crème fraîche.
A sharp, fermented aroma from short-chain fatty acids in aged cheese.
scale.science: Butyric and other short-chain fatty acids.

scale.meaning: A powerful, feet-like aroma of washed-rind or very ripe cheese.

children.label: Meat
children.summary: Aromas of cooked, cured and wild meat, from savory to gamey.

scale.meaning: A savory, protein-rich aroma from cooked meat and Maillard reaction products.
A salty, savory, slightly sweet aroma like ham, bacon or salami.
A dry, animal, slightly smoky aroma like old leather or aged wine.
A strong, wild aroma from game meats such as venison or mutton.

children.label: Seafood
children.summary: Aromas of the sea and of fish, from fresh sea air to fishy.

scale.meaning: A clean, salty-fresh aroma like sea air.
A green, iodine-tinged aroma like nori or kelp.
scale.science: Dimethyl sulfide and bromophenols.

scale.meaning: A sweet, briny aroma like oysters, shrimp or crab.
A strong aroma of fish that is no longer fresh.
scale.science: Trimethylamine increases as fish ages; acid (lemon) binds it and reduces the smell.

children.label: Fermented
children.summary: Aromas made by yeasts and microbes, from fresh dough to barnyard funk.

scale.meaning: A fresh, doughy aroma of live yeast or rising bread.
A heavy, sweet aroma of fruit starting to ferment.
A fruity, alcoholic aroma like wine, cider or fruit fermenting.
A wild, sour-fermented aroma like kimchi, kombucha or sour beer.
A strong, earthy-animal aroma like a stable, from wild yeasts.
scale.science: Ethylphenols from Brettanomyces yeast.

children.label: Off-Notes
children.summary: Aromas that are unpleasant, artificial, or indicate spoilage or contamination.

children.label: Stale & Oxidized
children.summary: Aromas of food that has aged or been exposed to air, from flat to rancid.

scale.meaning: A flat, tired aroma from food that has sat too long.
A dry, papery aroma, as in old beer or crackers.
scale.science: Trans-2-nonenal from slow fat oxidation.

scale.meaning: An unpleasant off-aroma from oxidized or hydrolyzed fats.
examples: oil used too long for frying
scale.science: Lipid oxidation produces hexanal and other aldehydes.

children.label: Musty & Moldy
children.summary: Aromas from microbes and damp, from cellar-like to putrid.

scale.meaning: A damp, stale aroma often from microbial activity or old storage.
scale.science: Trichloroanisole (TCA, 'corked' wine) and geosmin.

scale.meaning: An unpleasant fungal aroma indicating mold growth on food.
The sharp, sour aroma of spoiled dairy.
The strong, sickening smell of rotting food.
scale.science: Amines such as putrescine and cadaverine from protein breakdown.

children.label: Chemical
children.summary: Aromas that do not belong in food, from plastic to sulfurous.

scale.meaning: A chemical aroma like plastic wrap or a new container.
examples: water from a bottle left in the sun

scale.meaning: A sharp, nail-polish-remover aroma.
scale.science: Ethyl acetate in excess.

scale.meaning: A musky, sulfur aroma like light-struck beer.
examples: beer in clear bottles left in sunlight
scale.science: Light breaks down hop compounds into a skunk-like thiol.

scale.meaning: A sharp, egg-like aroma from hydrogen sulfide and sulfur compounds.
scale.science: Hydrogen sulfide; overcooked eggs and brassicas release it.

categories.label: Texture
categories.summary: The physical sensations experienced in the mouth when eating food, including hardness, softness, and surface properties.

children.label: Firmness & Chew
children.summary: How the food resists your teeth: how hard it is, how long it takes to chew, and how much it springs back.

children.label: Firmness
children.summary: The resistance of food to biting force or compression, from softest to hardest.

scale.meaning: An overly soft texture that has lost structural integrity.
scale.science: Cell walls (pectin) break down with overcooking or overripening.

scale.meaning: A texture that readily gives way to pressure without resistance.
A texture that is soft and easy to bite, yielding with little force.
scale.science: In meat, collagen converting to gelatin with slow cooking.

scale.meaning: A texture that offers moderate resistance to biting, holding its shape well.
A texture with high resistance to biting, requiring significant force.
A texture that does not give way or deform under pressure at all.

children.label: Chewiness
children.summary: How much chewing it takes before you can swallow, from a clean bite to gristly.

scale.meaning: Needs no chewing at all; it melts or breaks away, like shortbread or a ripe avocado.
A slight, pleasant resistance at the centre, like properly cooked pasta.
A texture requiring prolonged chewing, with good elasticity and cohesion.
scale.science: Gluten networks in bread; connective tissue in meat.

scale.meaning: Hard work to chew, as with overcooked or under-tenderized meat.
examples: squid cooked a few minutes too long

scale.meaning: Contains bits of connective tissue that resist chewing altogether.

children.label: Bounce
children.summary: How much the food springs back when you bite or press it.

scale.meaning: A wobbly, gel-like texture from gelatin or similar hydrocolloids.
A texture that rebounds after compression, like a sponge.
A pleasantly resilient, elastic chew, like mochi or tapioca pearls (the 'QQ' texture).
An overly elastic texture that resists being bitten through, like overcooked squid.

children.label: Crunch & Crumble
children.summary: How the food breaks, holds together, or sticks as you bite and chew it.

children.label: Crunch
children.summary: How food fractures when bitten, and how much sound and force it takes.

scale.meaning: A gentle snap with give, like lightly cooked vegetables.
A texture that shatters with a sharp sound and little resistance.
A texture that fractures with a loud sound and requires force to bite through.
A hard, glassy texture that shatters into shards, like toffee or hard candy.
scale.science: Sugar cooked to the hard-crack stage forms an amorphous glass.

children.label: Cohesiveness
children.summary: The degree to which food holds together and resists breaking apart.

scale.meaning: A texture that breaks apart easily into small pieces.
A texture that separates into thin, flat layers when bitten.
scale.science: Layers of fat between dough sheets turn to steam and separate the layers.

scale.meaning: A texture that holds together well without falling apart.
A soft, dense mass that clumps together as you chew, like underbaked bread.
A soft, elastic texture that sticks together and resists chewing.

children.label: Stickiness
children.summary: How much the food clings to your teeth, tongue and the roof of your mouth.

scale.meaning: Slightly sticky to the touch or tongue.
A texture that adheres to surfaces and teeth.
A thick paste that coats and clings to the roof of the mouth, like peanut butter.
So sticky it glues your teeth together, like caramel or overworked mashed potato.

children.label: Structure
children.summary: What the food is built from: how much air, what size of particles, and how fibrous.

children.label: Airiness
children.summary: How much air is built into the food, from dense to almost weightless.

scale.meaning: A tightly packed texture with little air, feeling heavy.
Noticeably less heavy than it looks.
A light, porous texture with significant air incorporation.
scale.science: Gas bubbles trapped by protein (egg, gluten) or fat networks.

scale.meaning: An exceptionally light, soft, cloud-like texture.
Mostly air held in a thin film, collapsing on the tongue, like mousse or meringue.

children.label: Grain
children.summary: The perceived size of solid particles in the food, from none to large lumps.

scale.meaning: A texture with no detectable particles or roughness.
A dry texture of very fine particles that may feel chalky.
A texture with fine, loose particles reminiscent of sand.
A texture with small, hard particles that are distinctly perceptible.
A texture with large, rough particles that are easily detected.
Uneven lumps or chunks in an otherwise smooth food.

children.label: Fibrousness
children.summary: How much the food is made of strands or fibers you can feel, from tender strands to woody.

scale.meaning: Comes apart in soft, tender strands, like pulled pork or slow-cooked beef.
Has noticeable fibers running through it, like celery or pineapple core.
Long fibers that catch in your teeth, like old green beans or melted cheese strings.
Hard, tough fibers that will not chew down, like old asparagus ends.

children.label: Moisture
children.summary: The degree to which food contains and releases water during consumption, from driest to juiciest.

scale.meaning: An extremely dry texture that is unpleasant and difficult to swallow.
A texture with low moisture content that absorbs saliva.
A texture with adequate water content, neither dry nor wet.
A texture that releases abundant moisture when bitten.
A richly moist texture that releases flavorful juices generously.

categories.label: Mouthfeel
categories.summary: How the food feels as it coats, fills and moves around the mouth.

children.label: Body
children.summary: The thickness and flow resistance of liquid or semi-liquid foods.

scale.meaning: A very thin, low-viscosity texture like water.
A low-viscosity texture that pours easily with little resistance.
Has noticeable weight and roundness in the mouth, like whole milk.
A high-viscosity texture that resists flow and pours slowly.
scale.science: Starches, gums and reduced proteins thicken by tangling water in long molecules.

scale.meaning: A dense, slow-flowing texture like syrup or honey.

children.label: Creaminess
children.summary: How smooth and luxurious the food feels across the tongue.

scale.meaning: Slippery-smooth and light, gliding across the tongue.
A smooth, rich texture from fat emulsions that coats the mouth.
An exceptionally smooth, soft, plush texture that feels luxurious in the mouth.

children.label: Richness
children.summary: The degree to which fat is present and perceived in food texture.

scale.meaning: Little perceptible fat; clean and light.
A full, satisfying fat texture that coats the mouth generously.
Luxuriously fatty and mouth-coating, like bone marrow or confit.
A texture with perceptible free oil that coats the mouth.
A texture with excess oil that feels heavy and leaves residue.

children.label: Slipperiness
children.summary: How slick or slimy the food feels, from smoothly slick to slimy.

scale.meaning: A smooth, slippery surface that glides easily, like a well-sauced noodle.
Hard to hold on the tongue, like jelly, aloe or soft tofu.
A thick, mucus-like coating, like okra, natto or raw egg white.
scale.science: Mucilage and other long sugar chains that hold water.

children.label: Astringency
children.summary: A drying, puckering sensation in the mouth caused by tannins and polyphenols.

scale.meaning: A sensation where moisture seems pulled from the mouth tissues.
A gripping astringency from tannin compounds, characteristic of red wine and strong tea.
scale.science: Tannins bind saliva proteins, removing their lubrication.

scale.meaning: An astringent sensation that makes the cheeks and gums feel contracted.
A coarse, sandpaper-like astringency on the palate.
So astringent the teeth and tongue feel coated in fur, like unripe persimmon.
scale.science: Unripe fruit holds more soluble tannin.

children.label: Carbonation
children.summary: The feel of bubbles in drinks and fermented foods.

scale.meaning: A faint prickle of tiny bubbles, just enough to lift the drink.
Lively, steady streams of fine bubbles.
Plenty of bubbles that pop noticeably on the tongue.
A sharp, needle-like prickle of bubbles on the tongue or cheeks.
Coarse, stinging carbonation that bites the throat.
scale.science: Dissolved CO2 turns to carbonic acid, which triggers sour and pain receptors.

categories.label: Heat & Sensation
categories.summary: Chemesthesis and temperature: the heat, cooling, tingling and thermal feel of food.

children.label: Pungent Heat
children.summary: Chemical burns that are felt, not tasted: chili on the tongue, mustard in the nose, alcohol in the throat.

children.label: Chili Heat
children.summary: How hot chili and pepper heat feels on the tongue, from a warm glow to painful.

scale.meaning: A gentle, spreading glow of heat, like ginger or cinnamon.
scale.science: Gingerols and shogaols in ginger.

scale.meaning: A pleasant, noticeable heat with a lively bite.
Strong heat that builds and fills the mouth.
An intense heat sensation from spicy compounds affecting mucous membranes.
scale.science: Capsaicin is fat-soluble: dairy and oil relieve the burn better than water.

scale.meaning: A sharp, painful heat that is hard to bear.

children.label: Nose Heat
children.summary: The sharp heat that rushes up the nose from mustard, horseradish and wasabi.

scale.meaning: A light, sharp prickle in the nose.
A sharp, rising heat in the nose and sinuses.
A strong rush of heat that clears the sinuses.
scale.science: Isothiocyanates are volatile, so they reach the nose and fire TRPA1 pain receptors there.

scale.meaning: So pungent it brings tears to the eyes.
examples: a lump of wasabi on its own

children.label: Alcohol Heat
children.summary: The warmth and burn of alcohol in drinks, sauces and desserts.

scale.meaning: A soft warmth spreading through the chest after swallowing.
A clear, noticeable alcohol lift on the nose and tongue.
Alcohol is front and centre, warming the whole mouth.
scale.science: Ethanol activates the same heat receptor (TRPV1) as chili.

scale.meaning: A rough alcohol burn that scratches the throat, as in young spirits.

children.label: Cooling
children.summary: A chemesthetic sensation of coolness that is felt, not a cold temperature, as from menthol in mint.

scale.meaning: A faint, calming coolness, like cucumber, aloe or a mild herb tea.
A clean, crisp coolness that freshens the breath, like spearmint.
A clear menthol chill across the tongue and nose.
scale.science: Menthol activates the cold receptor TRPM8 without lowering the temperature.

scale.meaning: A strong, almost cold-burn chill, like strong peppermint or eucalyptus.

children.label: Tingle & Numbing
children.summary: The buzzing, electric sensations of Sichuan pepper and similar plants.
children.science: Hydroxy-alpha-sanshool in Sichuan pepper makes touch nerves fire at about 50 Hz, felt as buzzing.

scale.meaning: A light, effervescent fizz on the lips and tongue.
examples: a light dusting of sichuan pepper

scale.meaning: A steady vibrating sensation, as if the lips are humming.
A sharp, battery-like zing.
The lips and tongue go partly numb for a while.

children.label: Temperature
children.summary: The thermal sensation of food as perceived in the mouth, affecting palatability.

children.label: Cold
children.summary: From lightly chilled to ice-cold.

scale.meaning: A food served slightly chilled, below room temperature.
Properly cold from the fridge.
A food served at a noticeably chilled temperature.
At or near freezing, with a numbing effect.

children.label: Warm
children.summary: From barely warm to too hot to eat.

scale.meaning: A food at a tepid temperature, barely warm.
examples: tepid coffee left on the desk

scale.meaning: A food served at a comfortably warm temperature.
A food served hot enough to feel very warm in the mouth.
Steaming; you need to blow on it before eating.
Hot enough to burn the mouth.
examples: pizza cheese straight from the oven

categories.label: Overall Impression
categories.summary: Holistic descriptors capturing the general character of a food's complete flavor experience.

children.label: Strength
children.summary: How loud the flavor is overall.

scale.meaning: A gentle, subtle overall flavor that is refined and not overpowering.
A moderate, understated flavor that is pleasant and unintimidating.
Clearly flavorful; you notice it right away.
A full-bodied, assertive flavor profile with strength and presence.
A powerful, concentrated flavor with strong impact on the palate.

children.label: Brightness
children.summary: How lively and fresh the flavor feels, from muted to vivid.

scale.meaning: Flavors are there but feel dull or flat.
A clean, lively flavor that invigorates and revitalizes the palate.
A vivid, lively flavor that stands out with clarity and freshness.
Bursting with vivid, high-contrast flavor.

children.label: Balance
children.summary: How well the flavors fit together, from clashing to seamless.

scale.meaning: The elements clash or stand apart instead of working together.
examples: a sour wine with a sweet dessert

scale.meaning: Soft-edged and smooth; nothing sticks out sharply.
No single element dominates; all components are in proportion.
All the elements work together and lift each other.
examples: a caprese salad with ripe tomatoes

children.label: Complexity
children.summary: How many distinct flavors you can pick out, and how they unfold.

scale.meaning: One clear flavor, straightforward and easy to name.
A flavor that reveals different notes in sequence on the attack, mid-palate, and finish.
A flavor profile with multiple distinct layers and dimensions that evolve on the palate.

categories.label: Finish
categories.summary: What stays with you after you swallow: how long the flavor lasts and what it leaves behind.

children.label: Length
children.summary: How long the flavor lasts after swallowing.

scale.meaning: Gone almost as soon as you swallow.
A brief echo of the flavor, then nothing.
Lingers a few seconds before fading.
Stays noticeably and keeps developing well after swallowing.
Still there long after; it may color the next bite.

children.label: Aftertaste
children.summary: What the finish leaves in the mouth, from clean to heavy.

scale.meaning: Leaves the palate fresh, with nothing behind.
A neat, sharp end that resets the palate, often from acidity or bubbles.
A film of fat or sugar stays on the tongue.
The flavor hangs on and weighs on the palate, often from sugar, fat or oak.
